Presidential RamblingsBy Steve Hansen
While Bruce continues to make a remarkable recovery, the Guild extends a big thank you to Claudia
Hayward and Bill Fowle for filling in for his dual role
as insurance liaison and Treasurer. Thank you Claudia. Thank you Bill.
My kind of demonstrator! I rang up Allan Cusworth a short while back and asked if he would be
interested in doing a demo for the Guild. Without
hesitation he jumped at it and quickly made the
arrangement to get re-certified as a Guild (lathe)
demonstrator. Allan gave an informative talk and
demonstration on turning, shaping and painting
“tantalizing tulips. It should go without saying that
organizations such as ours depend on our own
members to show us what they do and how they
do it. This is one of our prime mandates – to share.
Each of us has a skill or technique or pocket of
knowledge which others would benefit from. Everyone has something to share. And, it is fun to do so.
In fact, in-house presentations are the lifeblood of
every wood turning club. You do not need an invitation to do a presentation. It would be rather nice if
members would queue up to do them!
The President’s Challenge for November is a kitchen utensil.
Steve

Editor’s NotesBy Steve Fairbairn
In this month’s newsletter you’ll find the detailed
handouts for Allan Cusworth’s presentation on
turning tulips on the lathe. This month’s Member
Profile interview’s Scott Morgan. Shiela Balzer, our
Women In Turning liaison, is back with her ongoing
series about her journey as a new turner. I’ve also
reprinted a safety article from 20 years ago this
month on the potential hazards of CA glue which I
felt was as relevant today as it was 20 years ago.
Please consider contributing an article for our
newsletter. Our newsletter depends on contributions from our members.
Steve
Please email all Instant Gallery and President’s Challenge photos to
gallery@gvwg.ca by at least 3 days before the monthly meeting to ensure they are included in the gallery presentations.
In your email, please include as much information as possible on your
project such as species, dimensions, finish, special techniques, anecdotes, etc.
If you would like your photo to be considered as a newsletter cover
photo, please provide a high resolution photo in portrait format with a
clean background and foreground.

Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 4
This Month’s Cover
-Turning a Tulip Demonstration
By Allan Cusworth
Turning a Tantalizing Tulip
Demonstration Handout
GVWG Sept 28, 2023 - Allan Cusworth
Preparing the Blank
For this project, I selected a big leaf maple blank 2”
square by 4” long. The finished flower will be approximately 1¾” in diameter by 2¾” long. Measurements will need to be adjusted if you make one
of a different size.
Mark and dimple the centers on the ends of the
blank; mount it between centers and cut a tenon
on one end to fit your chuck jaws. Do not round it
off yet.
Preparing the Pistil and a Stem to Add Later
Pistil: Cut a piece of ¼” dowel 1” long, dye it brown
or black, color the tip with yellow acrylic paint and
let it dry.
Stem: Color a piece of Dollar Store ¼” dowel with
either green dye or acrylic paint. A green Bingo
dabber works too. Since Bingo dabbers are water
based, apply some nitro-cellulose sealer diluted
50/50 with lacquer thinner to seal the surface. If
using a natural finish, the dowel should be finished
to match the flower.
Shaping the Outside of the Tulip
Mount the square blank in a scroll chuck and line it
up using the center point of the live center in the
tailstock. Replace the live center with a Jacob’s®
chuck. Bore a hole, 2¼” deep with a ¾” Forstner
bit. Replace the Forstner bit with a ¼” drill bit and
bore a hole all the way through the blank.
Using a small cone on the live center in the tailstock for support, round off the blank making sure
you don’t catch the jaws of the chuck. Mark the
2¼” depth of the inside hole on the outside surface. Make another mark 2¾” from the tip to mark
the outside bottom of the tulip. This will provide a
½” base to allow for gluing the stem into the
bottom, as well as gluing the pistil inside.
Shape the outside of the tulip with an open or
closed petal design. Leave extra wood at the base
(Continued on page 5)

October 2023
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 5
for support when hollowing the inside.
Hollow out the inside following the outside profile
of the petal area just made. I use a Don Derry small
hollowing tool with an outrigger, but any hollowing
tool will work fine. Make sure you are cutting on,
or slightly above center. Make the inside bottom
concave to be more natural and for easier sanding.
Don’t make the petal area too thin; it increases the
chance of splitting when cutting them out later as
well as reducing the tendency of going through the
outside when hollowing. It’s a good idea to remove
the live center from the tailstock to protect your
elbow when hollowing or sanding.
Do the final shaping of the tip of the petal area using 80 grit sandpaper. Sand the inside to 220 grit,
using strips of sandpaper on a split dowel, or a
small foam ball covered with sandpaper on a stick.
Sand the outside surface to 220 grit to remove any
tool marks. Final touch up sanding of the outside
will be done later.
Laying Out and Cutting the Petals
Mark a ring on the outside surface showing the 2¼”
depth of the inside. Also mark rings at 1 7/8” from
the tip of the tulip to mark the bottom of the petals, and at 1 3/8” from the tip to mark the bottom
of the curve of the petals.
Line up the tool rest so a pencil can draw a line exactly on center using the point of the live center in
the tailstock.
See the separate handout for instructions to make
a petal layout cone. If making and even number of
petals, the locations can be marked by using your
lathe’s indexing feature, or by referring to the
spaces between the chuck jaws.
If using the petal layout cone, place it against the
point in the live center in the tailstock and carefully
bring it up to touch the rim of the petal area. Decide if you want to make four or five petals and
mark the rim where the black lines meet it for four
petals, or where the red lines meet it for five petals. I made four petals for this demonstration. Using the centered toolrest, draw straight lines from
the rim to the 1 7/8” ring on the tulip.
Remove the cone and make a mark by eye at the
midpoint at the tip between these lines just drawn
to identify each petal tip. Draw an arc from the
petal tip mark just made to the spot where the petal curve ends on the 1 3/8” circle. I like to use a
French curve, but free hand is OK too since not all
flower petals are symmetrical.
Cut along these curved petal lines with a small fine
tooth saw to the 1 3/8” ring on all petals. After all
petal curves are cut, continue to cut the slot from
the 1 3/8” ring to the 1 7/8” circle to complete the
rough shape of the petal. You can use the headstock spindle lock to hold the flower from spinning.
Finalize the petal shaping with strips of cloth sandpaper 80 to 220 grit. Paper back abrasives will tear
more easily. Make sure the edges of the petals are
smoothe.
Mark the 2 ¾” overall depth dimension on the outside of the tulip and continue shaping the outside
of the base. A little bead at the base provides a
little decoration. Don’t cut into the ¼” stem
mounting hole!
Finish sanding the outside to finished grit. I like 220
if painting or 320/400 if finishing naturally.
Finishing and Coloring
Finish the tulip on the lathe. Dye or paint the inside
and outside surfaces with your color of choice.
Shading with a complimentary color can be an added effect. Aniline dyes work well if you want the
grain to show through. So do acrylic paints. When
the color is dry, rub the tulip with extra-fine synthetic steel wool. Wipe the dust off with tack cloth.
Use “rattle can” spray lacquer, or spray polyurethane with the lathe spinning at about 350 rpm
and then slow the speed to 100 rpm to reduce the
tendency of runs. Apply three light coats, rub the
outside of the flower with extra-fine synthetic steel
wool between the first two and wipe it off with
tack cloth. Leave the last coat to dry and harden
completely. If a natural wood finish is preferred,
use only the spray lacquer or polyurethane. Note
that the stem and pistil should be finished naturally
(Continued from page 4)
(Continued on page 6)

October 2023
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 6
too. You could put a little dab of yellow acrylic
paint on the tip of the pistil.
After the finish has hardened part off the tulip off
close to the base. Sand the bottom and finish to
match the rest of the flower.
Assembling the Tulip
Glue the pistil about halfway into the inside of the
¼” hole drilled in the flower. I use a hemostat or
needle nosed pliers covered with masking tape to
protect the pistil end.
Glue the stem into the outside of the ¼” hole
meeting the pistil. You may need to use a hemostat
or other long nosed pliers covered with masking
tape to protect the yellow end of the pistil when
inserting the stem.
After the glue dries, your tulip is complete.
Tulip Petals Layout Marking Cone
Blank Specifications and Preparation
Mark & dimple centers on each end of a piece of
hard or soft wood 5” long x 3” square. Round off
the blank to exactly 2½” diameter. Accuracy is important here for later calculations. Mark a ring 3½”
from the tailstock end of the blank and cut a
groove. Turn a straight sided cone from the ring at
3½” towards the tailstock end making ¾” diameter
rounded nose. Leave the 1½” section straight and
the ring mark intact. I like to apply some nitrocellulose sanding sealer so the layout markings will not
run.
Laying Out Petal Location Lines
Five Petal Locations
Wrap a ¾” wide strip of paper around the blank at
the 3½” ring and mark where the paper overlaps
itself. Remove the strip of paper to mark five (5)
equal divisions.
The circumference of a 2½” diameter circle/blank is
7.85”. This is where accuracy of the diameter of
the blank is critical. Divide 7.85” by 5 = 1.57”, or 1
37/64” per division. Make a mark on the paper
strip every 1 37/64”.
Line up the tip of the toolrest with the point of the
live center in the tailstock so that a pencil will draw
a line on center.
Tape the paper strip around the straight, nontapered section of the cone at the 3½” ring mark
and mark the five (5) positions on the cone. Place
the toolrest at each position and draw a straight
line with a thin red marker from the 3½” ring to the
rounded nose.
Four Petal Locations
Mark the strip of paper using the same procedure
but with four (4) equal divisions. The positions will
be 1 31/32” per division, (7.85” circumference divide by 4 = 1.96”, or 1 31/32). Draw the straight
lines with a thin black marker.
(Continued from page 5)

Tell us about your background - how did you
get into woodturning?
I’ve always dabbled a bit in making things and it
started when I was very young. When I was about 6
my parents started building a cottage in Ontario
and my brother and I would get dragged along. We
would go exploring while they worked. Then in the
summer before I started grade 4 we moved and my
parents started to build a house in the country. My
brother and I spent every day going to the new
property for 8am. We would often take off and explore the country around the property, but usually
by the afternoon we would be called upon to help
with something. In the years to follow I learned
how to use a hammer, skillsaw, nail puller, mix
stucco, and that when you plant a tree the hole
had to be about 4 times bigger than the root ball
on the tree. At the time I didn’t enjoy a lot of the
work, but looking back I learned a lot and it certainly shaped who I am today. I didn’t realize till decades later that my dad had no previous building
skills. He was self-taught (Reader Digest building
book), in a time before the internet. But his mindset was I can do this. He read books, watched other
trades people working, asked questions, and
learned and those lessons have stuck with me.
My first foray into woodturning was in grade 7
woodshop class where I turned a bowl and a set of
wickets for cricket. After that I didn’t give it, another thought till 9 years ago when I saw Frank
Howarth on YouTube turning a bowl. From there I
went down the YouTube rabbit hole and became
mesmerized by the wet shavings that could be shot
across the shop and I decided that I needed to try
turning. It was around this same time that my
wife’s uncle passed away and he left me his woodshop. Unfortunately, the woodshop was in Ontario,
and it was too expensive to ship the tools out, so I
sold most of the tools and then used the money to
buy a lathe, bandsaw, chainsaw and a few other
things. Took a 1-day workshop with Ed Petty and I
was hooked.
Tell us about your workshop/studio.
My workspace is in my one car garage in my backyard. I built the garage myself with the intention of
it being a woodworking space and I’m happy to say
it has never seen a car in it. Unfortunately, it also
serves as a storage area for 5 bikes and all the odds
end that you collect when you do all the renos,
maintenance and upkeep on your home. My space
is set up for turning first, so I have clear access to
my lathe, bandsaw, and grinder. When I do other
woodworking, everything is on wheels, so I wheel
my grinding station and dust collector in front of
my lathe which then opens up space to my table
saw and jointer.
Last year we took over our basement, after having
tenants for 15 years and this gave me access to the
(Continued on page 8)
Guild Member Profile
- Scott Morgan
By Scott Morgan with Diana Dougherty

October 2023
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 8
unconditioned space under the concrete stairs
leading to our front porch and door. I added ridged
foam insulation to the inside walls and fully air
sealed the space, then added shelving and a dehumidifier, I now have great drying room for all my
green bowls, mills and cutting board blanks. The
only downside is that there is no floor drain so I
have to empty the dehumidifier ever 2-3 days
when the wood is really wet. This first batch of
wood that I dried in there was a success with almost no cracking.
What tools do you like using at your lathe?
I use traditional HSS turning tools. I’m certainly not
opposed to carbide; I just haven’t found a need yet
to use them. My go-to tool is a 5/8” bowl gouge.
Another favourite tool is my P&N detail gouge
which I much prefer over a spindle gouge. I suspect
the reason for that is that the first class I ever did
with the guild was when Michael Hosaluk presented. I didn’t realize I needed to bring tools to the
KMS day and turned up empty handed. Michael
graciously lent me his tools and I ended up using
his detail gouge for most of the day, I’ve been
hooked ever since.
What is your favourite wood?
If I have to choose, I really like cherry and red maple for bowls, but really, I’m happy with any of the
tighter grain hardwoods like maple, birch, beech,
or ash.
What finishes do you prefer using?
I prefer simple and easy to apply matte finishes, so
I generally go with an oil finish. The main finishes I
use are Tried and True Danish oil and Osmo Polyx
Oil. For both these finishes, a little goes a long way.
I’ve also used Odie’s Oil and I really liked it but it’s
expensive and it spoils quickly if the container you
keep it in 100% air tight.
Do you ever incorporate other materials into
your pieces?
So far my turning projects have all been wood although I have painted the outside of some of my
bowls with milk paint.
(Continued from page 7)
(Continued on page 9)
Drying Room
Peppermills

October 2023
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 9
What other types of woodworking or pursuits
do you have?
Growing up I was into sports and outdoor activities
(running, Nordic and Telemark skiing, canoeing,
camping, mountain biking). When I went to university I got into climbing (rock, ice and mountaineering) and that consumed most of my free time for
about 15 years till I had children, and my recreation
time became focused on them. It was then that I
started to do more woodworking and since then
I’ve done lots of projects such as Queen size bed,
wall lamps and lots of other furniture in our house.
Most of the projects are practical based, meaning I
needed something for our house and couldn’t find
what we were looking for, so I made it. The kids are
getting older now, mid to late teenagers, and more
independent
which
means
in
addition
to
woodturning I’ve been able to get out rock climbing and backcountry skiing again.
What inspires you – where do you get your
ideas from?
There isn’t one person or thing that inspires me. I
get inspiration from many places, my family, and
friends, and work I see in magazines or on Instagram. As much as Instagram can be a major time
suck, it is a great tool to see what others are doing
all over the world. It provides us access to amazing
artists around the world both professional and amateurs. I also find that so many people on Instagram are willing to answer questions. I built my
drying room after asking an Irish production turner
a question about his. He provided a very detailed
response, and we ended messaging back and forth
on Instagram for a whole afternoon.
Who has been the greatest influence on your
work and where do you usually display and/or
sell your work?
My family have definitely influenced my work and
the extent to which I turn. When I initially started
turning it was definitely for fun and it still is mainly.
But as I started turning bowls, and found how both
frustrating and satisfying it was, I was set on figuring the process out and getting good at it. So of
course the bowls starting piling up. We gave lots
away as gifts to family, friends, then teachers and
tutors. What took one day to make, started to take
half a day then slowly less and less time. One day
while visiting a farmers market my kids suggested
that I should sell my things and that planted a seed.
Eventually I took the plunge in the fall of 2018. I
have also sold a bit on Etsy, but most of my work is
sold at weekend craft shows and through word of
mouth.
What is the most challenging piece that you
have made so far?
Honestly, bowls are still my most challenging pieces. I’ve probable turned 500-600 and I still have
lots to improve on. To get less tear out or no bump
between sections as you hollow out the inside of a
bowl in stages, to get a smooth finish on the inside
bottom of a deep bowl. One thing that keeps me
turning is a desire to perfect/master the process
and design.
What is your favorite project to date?
About a year ago I saw a fellow named Andrew
McCarn on YouTube turn a bowl with handles on
the rim and was quite taken by his bowl. While
roughing turning some bowls last winter I left a few
thicker than normal so I could try. Last month I finally got around to giving it a go and really enjoyed
the process. It really wasn’t anything difficult, but it
(Continued from page 8)

was different than what I normally do so ending up
being very satisfying. I definitely plan on turning a
few more.
Where do you see your work going in the future?
I will continue to make bowls and pepper/salt mills
as I sell lots of these. Last year I bought some hollowing tools and have made a few small hollow
forms, and I would very much like to do more.
There are several turners that do some amazing
embellishing of spheres, folks like Neil Turner,
Vivien Grandouiller, Felix Brason of Turner and
Chuck, Andy Phillip and Dale Larson. I really enjoy
making spheres and would like to experiment with
embellishing them. Lots of projects in the back of
my mind, just have to find the time!

CA Glue Hazard WarningBy Wayne Pilchak
After a recent discussion about the hazard potential of large bottles of CA glue, a qualified expert on
Cyanoacrylate glue has asked me to bring the following safety information to the attention of
woodworkers:
Cyanoacrylate is unlike the other woodworking adhesives we use and it requires some special handling. CA in the bottle is a very small, very reactive
molecule. It doesn’t become an adhesive until it
cures. Curing involves a chemical reaction between
the small molecules to make very large molecules
(polymer). The special properties of polymers enable cured CA to become an adhesive. The curing
reaction gives off large quantities of heat. For example, less than 4 oz of CA will produce 15,000 calories of heat during curing. The heat given off by a
small dab of CA curing slowly is dissipated and it is
not noticed, but if a larger quantity of CA cures
quickly, enough heat can be given off to boil and /
or decompose the CA with the production of noxious and probably toxic fumes as well as the possibility of fire or explosion.
An accelerator (catalyst) will cause CA to quickly
cure and lead to these potential hazards. In addition to the accelerator designed to cause CA to
quickly cure, many other substances act as accelerators. Many dyes will be excellent accelerators ,
and even water or glass can cause CA to cure rapidly. An extremely tiny amount of accelerator can
lead to the rapid cure of a whole bottle of CA. The
bottle would explode if it rapidly cured. To avoid
possible problems with CA don’t store large quantities, at least in the same bottle. Don’t ever add anything to CA unless you first test with a very small
quantity of CA to see if the additive is an accelerator. The test should be done with good ventilation
in case there is rapid cure, which leads to boiling,
fumes and possibly fire. Don’t transfer CA to a
different container from which it was originally
packaged. The new container could contain something that could act as an accelerator.
Bottom line: Be cautious handling anything more
than a drop of CA and never add anything to a larger quantity of CA that could lead to a rapid cure.
This article is reprinted from the October 2003
GVWG Newsletter.

Another Baby Step or Two By Sheila Balzer
-WIT Liaison
Since I have joined the world of woodturning community, I have heard many turners express how
classes are so much better to do in person, and
how much people gained form the experience of
getting to work with a visiting demonstrator directly in a class. Recently an invitation was fanned out
to all members in the GVWG that the FVWG would
be hosting such a weekend with Elizabeth Weber
doing a Thursday evening meeting, a Friday all day
class and a Saturday full day demonstration. Clearing other commitments, I managed to participate
in two of the three events.
I met Elizabeth online during one of the WIT Exchanges and ever since I have kept and eye on
what she has been up to. For example, she and
Nicole MacDonald became the 2023 Artist Showcase Awardees for the AAW’s Professional Outreach Program (POP) and attended and demonstrated at the 2023 AAW Symposium in Louisville,
Kentucky.
But now, given the FVWG hosting a weekend education event, here was my opportunity to meet
Elizabeth in person and learn from her explorations. I already knew much about her so what was
shared at the Thursday FVWG guild meeting I had
mostly heard before, but Elizabeth is an engaging
storyteller, so it was a pleasure to hear it again.
Elizabeth had also been a guest on Pat Carroll’s,
Meet the Woodturner. There are plenty of people
who know her worldwide now, but not so many in
our area knew her and the class that got hosted
was on the smallish side, especially given it was
finally an in-person class with a visiting demonstrator. Curious!
For a while now I’ve heard various takes and laments on in-person classes…fewer demonstrators
are wanting to travel to come teach but when one
is offered, there does not seem to be a hungry appetite for people to go and see them. Very curious!
I’m so very glad that I had the opportunity to make
it happen.
Being in a class
where we could
see, learn, play,
bounce ideas off
others, meet new
turners with fresh
perspectives, and
see an interesting
facility
where
wood gets process
into a variety of
forms for makers
to create was very
exciting. Sure, others may have little issue of
putting a carving gouge to a chunk of wood…but it
blew my mind, that for the purpose of the embellishments we might want to achieve, one had to
use the gouge ACROSS the grain, and not with it.
And while in my shop at home, I have been so focussed on “making” something, that I left out the
process to experiment with what it might look like
to try to make the same embellishment in different
ways…hand carving tool vs. power carver vs. pyrography. I have all the toys, thanks to seeing demonstrations online hosted by our guild, like from Donna Zils Banfield, but the day with Elizabeth everyone who attended just went for it and played.
So far, I am favouring the hand tools, but can appreciate that each has their own merit. This experience is bringing me a baby step closer to executing the images in my mind, and scribbles in my
book to be one step closer to evolving and coming
to life.
Another baby step was helping KMS celebrate 40
years as they hosted a big sale and events throughout their chain. Richard, Dan B. and Dan M. and I
did three days of demonstrations in their Coquitlam location.
Given some of the take aways from the class with
Elizabeth, my first day at the lathe I opted to turn a
bud vase on the new protype of the Nova Neptune
(Continued on page 12)

October 2023
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 12
and Dan M. turned pens. Meanwhile Dan B. and
Richard turned bowls on the Nova Nebula. The second afternoon I crafted a honey dipper for Doug to
gift to his wife. It was so much fun being teased for
taking so long (can’t rush an Artist!), but playing,
crafting, and talking to those who stopped by and
were curious about making stuff. This included one
of my piano students who went home with a diamond, honing compound, a hunk of leather and a
Pfeil carving knife so she could complete a high
school woodshop project with a much better tool
than a hobby knife. It also included the spouse of
one of the Dogwood woodworkers I know. Her
name is Diane, and I suspect we will soon be become crazy making women as her glass pieces is
something I want to learn, and she is very curious
about woodturning too.
But the end of the day on Friday, Chris from KMS
got all choked up as Richard announced his retirement from the KMS events (apparently, he has said
that before). Chris then shared a bunch of fond
memories of experiences he had with Richard and
reflected how much he was going to miss him. But
before Richard left for the day, we managed to get
a photo of us together…him in his very experienced
smock and me in my shinny and new smock I wore
for this very first time.
Like some have heard me declare “I’m not a bowl
turner” (but now I do turn bowls), I had also said
I’m not a pen turner, although I did make one a
while back in Gary’s shop. Well Dan M. has inspired me to change that as he and I worked
through the process, ever so slowly, and had a
blast making a pen with silver and birch. As I
rushed home from his shop to teach my music students of course I showed them what I made. Each
were very much impressed, especially how shinny
and smooth it was. They really liked it. (Sevenyear-olds give it to you straight.) Clearly, so do I.
So, baby steps continue as I strive and thrive. I
have a whole bunch more pens to make as well as
making those visions in my head and scribbled on
paper. Again, I gush with gratitude for all the people who continue to push, share, and support me
on this wonderous ride of woodturning.

Safety Guidelines for WoodturningYou mostly turn alone so safety is YOUR responsibility
 Always wear safety goggles or safety
glasses that include side protectors.
Use a full face shield for bowl, vessel, or
any turning involving chucks and faceplates.
 Use a combination of dust mask, air filtration helmet, proper ventilation, and/
or dust collection system as appropriate. Fine particles from a grinder and
wood dust are harmful to your respiratory system.
 Wear hearing protection during extended periods of turning.
 Turn the lathe off before adjusting the
tool rest or tool rest base, i.e., banjo.
 Always remove chuck keys, adjusting
wrenches, and knockout bars immediately after use. Never leave them in
place, even for a moment.
 Tie back long hair and avoid loose
clothing, jewelry, or any dangling objects that may catch on rotating parts
or accessories.
 When using a faceplate, be certain the
workpiece is solidly mounted with stout
screws (#10 or #12 sheet metal screws
as a minimum). Do not use dry wall or
deck screws.
 When turning between centres, be certain the workpiece is firmly mounted
between the headstock driving centre
and tailstock centre.
 Ensure the belt guard or cover is in
place.
 Check that all locking devices on the
tailstock and tool rest assembly (rest
and base) are tight before operating the
lathe.
 Ensure the blank is securely fastened.
 Rotate your workpiece backwards by
hand to make sure it clears the toolrest
and bed before turning the lathe on.
 Stay clear of the areas directly behind
and in front of the workpiece, they are
the most likely areas for a piece to travel as it comes off the lathe. A good safety habit is to step out of this zone when
turning on the lathe, keeping your hand
on the switch in case you need to turn
the machine off. When observing someone else turn, stay out of these zones.
 Always check the speed of the lathe before turning it on. Use slower speeds
for larger diameters or rough pieces
and higher speeds for smaller diameters and pieces that are balanced. Always start a piece at a slower speed until the workpiece is balanced. If the
lathe is shaking or vibrating, lower the
speed. If the workpiece vibrates, always
stop the machine to verify why. As a
starting point, consult your operator’s
manual for recommended speeds for a
particular lathe. Ensure the lathe speed
is compatible with the size of the blank.
 Exercise extra caution when using stock
(Continued on page 38)

October 2023
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 38
with cracks, splits, checks, bark pockets,
knots, irregular shapes, or protuberances. Beginners should avoid these types
of stock until they have greater
knowledge of working such wood.
 Hold turning tools securely on the
toolrest, holding the tool in a controlled
but comfortable manner. Always contact the tool rest with the tool before
contacting the wood.
 Note that, when running a lathe in reverse, it is possible for a chuck or faceplate to unscrew unless it is securely
tightened or locked on the lathe spindle.
 Know your capabilities and limitations.
An experienced woodturner is capable
of lathe speeds, techniques, and procedures not recommended for beginning
turners.
 Always remove the tool rest before
sanding, finishing, or polishing operations.
 Don’t overreach, keep proper footing,
and keep your balance at all times.
 Keep your lathe in good repair. Check
for damaged parts, alignment, binding
of moving parts, and other conditions
that may affect its operation.
 Keep tools sharp and clean for better
and safer performance. Don’t force a
dull tool. Don’t use a tool for a purpose
for which it was not designed or intended.
 Consider your work environment. Don’t
use a lathe in damp or wet locations.
Do not use in presence of flammable
liquids or gases, and always keep a fully
-charged fire extinguisher close at
hand. Keep your work area well lit.
 Stay alert. Watch what you are doing.
Pay close attention to unusual sounds
or vibrations. Stop the lathe to investigate the cause. Don’t operate machines
when you are tired or under the influence of drugs or alcohol.
 Guard against electric shock. Inspect
electric cords for damage. Avoid the
use of extension cords.
 Never leave the lathe running unattended. Turn power off. Don’t leave
lathe until it comes to a complete stop.
 Many accidents to woodturners occur
while using saws, especially band and
chain saws. Learn and follow the safety
guidelines for this equipment.
For more information on woodturning
safety please visit the AAW’s Woodturning Safety webpage.
